name: Bronchi
func: Branching airways that carry air from the trachea into each lung, splitting again and again into smaller tubes. Their muscle can tighten or relax to control airflow, and their lining cleans the air.

levels.kid:
At the bottom of your windpipe, the tube splits into two smaller tubes, like an upside-down letter Y. These are the **bronchi**. One goes to your left lung and one goes to your right lung.

Inside each lung they keep splitting, again and again, like the branches of a tree getting thinner and thinner. That's why doctors call it the **bronchial tree**. The tiniest twigs are called **bronchioles**, and at their ends are the little air balloons where oxygen goes into your blood.

The bronchi have rings of cartilage to keep them open and a thin layer of muscle around them. In people with **asthma**, that muscle squeezes too tight and the tubes get swollen and goopy, so it's hard to breathe and they might wheeze.
levels.hs:
The trachea divides at the **carina** (about **T4/T5**, the sternal angle) into the **right and left main (primary) bronchi**. Each enters its lung at the **hilum**, together with the pulmonary artery and veins.

The **right main bronchus** is shorter (about 2.5 cm), wider and more vertical. The **left main bronchus** is longer (about 5 cm) and more horizontal, because it must pass under the **arch of the aorta** and in front of the **esophagus** and descending aorta to reach the left lung.

Each main bronchus splits into **lobar (secondary) bronchi**, one per lobe: three on the right (upper, middle, lower) and two on the left (upper, lower). These then split into **segmental (tertiary) bronchi**, one for each bronchopulmonary segment.

Branching continues for about **23 generations** in total. The first 16 or so form the **conducting zone**, which moves, warms, humidifies and filters air but doesn't exchange gas (this volume, about 150 mL, is the anatomical dead space). The final generations form the **respiratory zone**, where gas exchange happens.

Bronchi contain cartilage plates and smooth muscle. **Bronchioles** (under about 1 mm) have no cartilage, so smooth muscle tone controls their width.
levels.college:
The **right upper lobe bronchus** leaves the right main bronchus only about 2 cm below the carina, above the right pulmonary artery, so it is called the **eparterial bronchus**. The rest of the right main bronchus continues as the **bronchus intermedius**, which gives the middle and lower lobe bronchi. On the left, the upper lobe bronchus also supplies the **lingula** (the left's equivalent of the middle lobe).

Structure changes as airways narrow:
- **Bronchi**: irregular cartilage plates (not C-rings), a spiral smooth muscle layer, seromucous glands and pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.
- **Bronchioles**: no cartilage or glands, relatively more smooth muscle, epithelium thinning to simple columnar then cuboidal, goblet cells replaced by **club cells**.
- **Terminal bronchioles**: last purely conducting airways.
- **Respiratory bronchioles**: first airways with alveoli budding from their walls.

The functional unit beyond a terminal bronchiole is the **acinus**.

Bronchial width is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. **Parasympathetic** (vagal) fibres release acetylcholine on **M3 muscarinic receptors**, constricting the muscle and increasing mucus. **Sympathetic** innervation of airway smooth muscle itself is sparse, but **β2-adrenergic receptors** respond to circulating adrenaline and relax it; this is how inhaled β2-agonist relievers work.

The **bronchial arteries** (usually one on the right from a posterior intercostal artery, two on the left from the aorta) feed the bronchial walls. Because airway resistance falls as total cross-sectional area grows, most resistance actually sits in the **medium-sized bronchi**, not the tiny bronchioles.
levels.phd:
**Airway resistance** follows Poiseuille-type behaviour (resistance rises steeply as radius falls, roughly to the fourth power for laminar flow), but flow in the large airways is partly turbulent. Because the small airways are so numerous and in parallel, their total resistance is low in health, which is why early small-airway disease is "silent" on standard tests.

Small airways are held open by **radial traction** from attached alveolar walls. In **emphysema**, destruction of those walls removes the tethering, so airways collapse during forced expiration (**dynamic airway compression**), causing air trapping.

In **asthma**, the core immunology is often **type 2 inflammation**: epithelial alarmins (**TSLP, IL-33, IL-25**) activate **ILC2s** and **Th2 cells**, which release **IL-4** (IgE class switching), **IL-5** (eosinophil survival) and **IL-13** (goblet cell metaplasia, airway hyperresponsiveness). Mast cells cross-linked by IgE release histamine, leukotrienes (LTC4/D4/E4) and prostaglandin D2, causing acute bronchospasm. Chronic **remodelling** includes subepithelial fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, and mucus gland enlargement. Modern biologic therapies target individual pieces of this pathway (IgE, IL-5, IL-4Rα, TSLP).

Airway smooth muscle contraction runs through Gq-coupled receptors → IP3 → calcium release → calmodulin → **myosin light chain kinase**, plus a **Rho-kinase** calcium-sensitisation pathway. β2 receptors act via Gs → cAMP → PKA, which reduces calcium and myosin phosphorylation.

**Club cells** secrete **club cell secretory protein (CC16)**, detoxify inhaled substances with cytochrome P450 enzymes and act as local stem cells. Bronchial **neuroendocrine cells**, clustered as neuroepithelial bodies, sense oxygen and are the likely origin of **small cell** and **carcinoid** tumours.
levels.expert:
**Exam**: **wheeze** (a musical, mostly expiratory sound) means narrowed airways, as in asthma, COPD or a foreign body. A **localised fixed wheeze** suggests a single obstruction, such as a tumour or inhaled object. In a severe asthma attack a **"silent chest"** is ominous: so little air moves that wheeze disappears.

**Tests**: **spirometry** shows obstruction (FEV1/FVC reduced). Significant improvement after a bronchodilator supports asthma; fixed obstruction fits COPD. **Peak flow** tracks variability.

**Bronchiectasis** is permanent dilation of bronchi from repeated infection and inflammation (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, after severe infection). Patients cough up large volumes of sputum daily. High-resolution CT shows the **signet ring sign** (an airway wider than its accompanying artery) and **tram-track** lines.

**Foreign body aspiration**, common in toddlers, usually lodges in the **right main or bronchus intermedius**. Unilateral air trapping on expiratory films is a clue; rigid **bronchoscopy** removes it. In a lying patient, aspirated material tends to enter the **posterior segment of the right upper lobe** or the **superior segment of the right lower lobe**, the classic sites of **aspiration pneumonia** in people with reduced consciousness, including neurosurgical patients.

**Lung cancer**: **squamous cell** and **small cell** carcinomas tend to arise centrally from large bronchi, while adenocarcinoma is usually peripheral. **Carcinoid tumours** are endobronchial lesions seen at bronchoscopy. Bronchoscopy with **endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS)** biopsies mediastinal nodes for staging.

**Surgical**: a **sleeve lobectomy** removes a lobe with a cuff of main bronchus and rejoins the ends, sparing lung. The feared complication after lung resection is a **bronchopleural fistula**.

keyPoints: Trachea splits at the carina into right and left main bronchi
Right main bronchus is short, wide and vertical; left passes under the aortic arch
About 23 generations of branching: conducting then respiratory zone
Bronchioles lack cartilage; smooth muscle sets their width
M3 constricts, β2 relaxes airway smooth muscle
Wheeze = narrowed airways; a silent chest in asthma is dangerous

test.q: Which airway is called the eparterial bronchus?
test.explain: The right upper lobe bronchus leaves above the right pulmonary artery.
Bronchioles have no cartilage, so their width depends on smooth muscle and on traction from surrounding lung.

test.q: Airway smooth muscle relaxes when adrenaline acts on β_ receptors (type the receptor).
test.explain: β2-adrenergic receptors relax bronchial smooth muscle via cAMP.

test.q: On high-resolution CT, an airway wider than its neighbouring artery is called the:
test.explain: The signet ring sign is a key CT clue to bronchiectasis.

test.q: The ridge at the tracheal bifurcation is the ______.
test.explain: The carina sits at about T4/T5 and is very cough-sensitive.
